title: Introduction to energy production in the mitochondria
canonical_question: How do mitochondria produce energy for the cell?
summary: Cellular respiration converts nutrients into ATP.
Most ATP is made in the mitochondrion.

sections.heading: What the mitochondrion does
sections.body_md: The mitochondrion is the part of a cell where most of its usable energy is made. It takes the energy stored in food molecules, mostly sugars and fats, and repackages it into a small molecule called ATP. Cells spend ATP to move, build, and signal, so a steady supply matters.

sections.heading: From food to ATP
sections.body_md: Breaking down food happens in stages. Sugars are first split in the fluid of the cell, and the fragments are then fed into the mitochondrion. Inside, a cycle of reactions strips high-energy electrons from these fragments and hands them to carrier molecules.

sections.heading: Why the mitochondrion is built the way it is
sections.body_md: A mitochondrion has two membranes. The inner one is folded into ridges that pack a large surface into a small space. Those folds hold the machinery that turns the electron supply into ATP, so more surface means more output.

sections.heading: The payoff: ATP
sections.body_md: ATP acts like a rechargeable battery. When a cell needs energy it breaks one bond in ATP and releases a usable burst; the spent molecule is then recharged in the mitochondrion. Because the pool is recycled constantly, a cell keeps only a small amount on hand at any moment.

key_points: Most of a cell usable ATP is produced in the mitochondrion.
Food energy is transferred to electron carriers, then to ATP.
The folded inner membrane holds the energy-converting machinery.
